newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Pou Chen denies bank investment in China.
newsitem.headline: Pou Chen denies bank investment in China.

text.p: Taiwan footwear maker Pou Chen Corp, whose shares tumbled on Wednesday over the government's pledge to clamp down on illegal China investments, has denied it invested in a bank in China, a newspaper reported on Thursday.
"Pou Chen is a listed company. It understands clearly the government's policies and regulations," the firm's president Tsai Nan-feng told the Economic Daily News in an interview.
"It will not secretly go to the mainland to invest in banking business when the (government's) policy still prohibits such investment," Tsai told the newspaper.

A Chinese central bank official told Reuters last week that China had approved a Taiwan company's application to set up the first Taiwan-invested bank in Shanghai, but did not name the firm. Taiwan media identified the company as Pou Chen, but company officials had refused comment on the reports. Tsai's interview with the Economic Daily was the company's first public comment.
Taiwan's economics ministry on Wednesday urged local firms to stop unauthorised investments in rival communist China and vowed to ferret out and punish any illegal investments.
The commission warned local firms not to set up banks in China a day after the visiting mainland official confirmed that the one Taiwan company already had done so.
Taiwan media named Pou Chen owner Tsai Chi-chien and his brother Tsai Nan-feng as the financiers behind the planned Shanghai bank, First Sino Bank.
"Pou Chen and its subsidaries did not invest in the First Sino Bank," Tsai said.
He added other members of the Tsai family also were not involved in the bank project.
"These rumours are only speculation," Tsai said.
Pou Chen, a major investor in mainland footwear business, would consider investing in China's banking business if the government lifts its ban, Tsai said.
Taiwan has banned direct contact with China since the Nationalists fled to the island after losing a civil war on the mainland in 1949.
After one hour of trade, Pou Chen jumped T$5.5 or 4.56 percent to T$126.
